Problem 383. Locating a point by constraints: case 3
Coordinates turn location into numbers. Multiple spatial clues can be treated as simultaneous constraints.
A point P lies on an integer grid with x,y from 0 to 6. It satisfies x+y=10 and x−y=-2.
A location is valid only if it satisfies every stated equation and inequality at the same time.
Which coordinate(s) can P occupy? Is the solution unique?
1. List pairs satisfying x+y=10. 2. Keep only those also satisfying x−y=-2. 3. The remaining set is [(4, 6)].
A constraint problem is solved by satisfying all conditions together, not one at a time independently.

N3. Earth, Sun, seasons, and local time
Problem 386. Earth, sunlight, and local time: case 1
Earth–Sun relationships explain broad patterns such as day length and local time, but a problem should state the simplified model it expects children to use.
For this classroom model, Eastport is 1 time zone(s) east of Westport. Each zone east is one hour later. At Westport it is 10:00.
Moving east adds one hour per stated time zone; moving west subtracts. Use the given model only.
What local time is it in Eastport?
1. Time difference is +1 hour(s) because Eastport is east. 2. 10+1=11 (mod 24).
A model supports only the conclusions encoded in its rules; seasonal light does not automatically determine daily weather.
Rule-based astronomical/time-zone model; apply signed offsets or seasonal relation.

Problem 389. Earth, sunlight, and local time: case 4
Earth–Sun relationships explain broad patterns such as day length and local time, but a problem should state the simplified model it expects children to use.

Use this simplified model: Earth’s axis is tilted. In the Northern Hemisphere, days are generally longer around June than around December. Compare June and December for the same place. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 12:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.
Use the stated seasonal relation; do not infer daily weather from season. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.
Which of the two months has the longer daylight period in this model, and can that fact alone tell us whether it will rain? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?

1. Apply the stated tilt-season relation. 2. June has the longer daylight period in the Northern Hemisphere. 3. The rule contains no information about rainfall, so rainfall cannot be deduced. Cross-domain check: 12+2=14, so the team finishes at 14:00.
June has longer daylight; rainfall cannot be determined from this fact alone. Cross-domain answer: 14:00.

Problem 391. Reservoir stock and flow: case 1
Many geographic and civic quantities are stocks and flows: water in a reservoir, people in a city, or goods in a warehouse.
A reservoir starts with 30 water units. Each day 5 units flow in and 5 units flow out. Assume these rates stay constant for 4 days.
Stock at the end = starting stock + total inflow − total outflow. Flow is an amount per time period; stock is the amount currently stored.
How much water is stored after 4 days? Is the stock increasing or decreasing each day?
1. Daily net change=5−5=0. 2. Over 4 days, net change=4×0=0. 3. End stock=30+(0)=30.
Do not confuse a stored amount with a rate of change; conservation links them.
